bigPicture.subtitle: The Letter That Skipped the Thank You
paragraphs: Paul never opened a letter to a church without first lifting his voice to God over the people about to read it. To a congregation in the imperial capital he had never visited: “First, I thank my God through Jesus Christ for all of you, that your faith is proclaimed throughout the whole world” (Romans 1:8). To Corinth — a church with factions, a man sleeping with his father's wife, and drunkenness at the Lord's table — he still wrote, “I always thank my God concerning you, for the grace of God which was given you in Christ Jesus” (1 Corinthians 1:4). To that same church a second time, after they had broken his heart and half of them had gone over to his rivals, the thanksgiving turned into a blessing but the praise still came before the pain: “Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Father of mercies and God of all comfort” (2 Corinthians 1:3). Now open Galatians. There is a greeting in verse 3. There is a doxology in verse 5 — “to whom be the glory forever and ever. Amen.” And then, before the ink is dry on that Amen: “I marvel that you are so quickly deserting him who called you in the grace of Christ to a different ‘good news’” (1:6). No thanks. No warm-up. No I remember you in my prayers. Of every letter Paul wrote to a church, this is the only one with no thanksgiving in it at all — and that silence is the loudest thing on the page. Marvel is θαυμάζω (thaumázō, G2296), to be staggered, to stand there with your mouth open. Deserting is μετατίθημι (metatíthēmi, G3346), a word for changing sides — the vocabulary of a soldier walking across the field to the enemy's camp while the battle is still going on. A house was on fire and Paul would not make small talk in the doorway.

Here is what had happened. Paul had walked into those towns with one message, and Luke preserved its shape for us from the very first sermon he preached in Galatian territory: “Be it known to you therefore, brothers, that through this man is proclaimed to you remission of sins, and by him everyone who believes is justified from all things, from which you could not be justified by the law of Moses” (Acts 13:38–39). Everyone who believes. Justified from all things. Then Paul moved on — and other teachers walked in behind him. They did not deny Jesus. They would have signed every line of the creed. They simply said He was not quite enough: believe, yes, and be circumcised, and take up the calendar, and then you will really belong. Paul refuses to file that under secondary difference. He calls it a different kind of gospel — ἕτερος (héteros, G2087), other in kind, a different species altogether — and then in the very next breath denies that any such thing exists: “and there isn't another ‘good news.’ Only there are some who trouble you, and want to pervert the Good News of Christ” (1:7), where another is ἄλλος (állos, G243), another of the same sort. There is no second gospel. There is the gospel, and there is a counterfeit wearing its clothes. So he says the unthinkable, and then says it twice so nobody can claim he was carried away: “But even though we, or an angel from heaven, should preach to you any ‘good news’ other than that which we preached to you, let him be cursed” (1:8). Cursed is ἀνάθεμα (anáthema, G331) — devoted to destruction, handed over, banned. Paul puts himself first on the list and an archangel second. That is not arrogance. It is a man saying: the message is not mine to edit, and if I ever edit it, burn my letters too.

These are almost certainly the churches of southern Galatia — Pisidian Antioch, Iconium, Lystra and Derbe — the towns Paul and Barnabas evangelised on the first missionary journey in Acts 13 and 14, planted at enormous personal cost and revisited on the way home. That places the letter around AD 48 or 49, most likely just before the Jerusalem Council of Acts 15, which would make Galatians the earliest surviving letter Paul ever wrote and quite possibly the oldest Christian document in existence. Some scholars date it later, around AD 53–55, and address it to ethnic Galatia further north; but the southern, early reading fits the geography Luke actually gives us, and it explains a silence that is otherwise inexplicable — Paul is fighting for his life on precisely the question the Jerusalem Council decided, and he never once cites the Council's ruling. He would have. It had not happened yet. Sit with that. The first thing the church ever wrote down, as far as we can tell, was not a devotional and not a manual of church order. It was a defence of grace with the safety off. And it was written by a man whose body still carried the receipts: at Lystra, one of these very towns, a mob stoned him and dragged him outside the city thinking he was dead (Acts 14:19). He gets to the end of this letter and writes, “From now on, let no one cause me any trouble, for I bear the marks of the Lord Jesus branded on my body” (6:17). Marks is στίγμα (stígma, G4742) — the brand burned into a slave's skin to show whose he was. Paul's scars are his ownership papers, and he is done arguing about credentials with men whose main concern is avoiding persecution (6:12).

The letter moves in three movements of two chapters each, and you can feel the temperature in every one. Chapters 1 and 2 are autobiography used as evidence: the gospel did not come to him from a committee — “not from men, nor through man, but through Jesus Christ, and God the Father, who raised him from the dead” (1:1); Arabia, then Damascus, then three years before he ever met Peter; then fourteen years before he laid his message before the Jerusalem leaders, where Titus, a Greek, walked in uncircumcised and walked out uncircumcised (2:3) despite “the false brothers secretly brought in, who stole in to spy out our liberty which we have in Christ Jesus, that they might bring us into bondage” (2:4). And it climaxes in a dining room in Antioch, where Peter — who had eaten happily with Gentile believers until men arrived from James — quietly slid down the table to the safe end, and took everyone with him: “And the rest of the Jews joined him in his hypocrisy; so that even Barnabas was carried away with their hypocrisy” (2:13). Even Barnabas. The one man who had vouched for Paul when the whole church was still afraid of him. Chapters 3 and 4 are the argument itself, and they open not with a syllogism but with a slap across the face: “Foolish Galatians, who has bewitched you not to obey the truth, before whose eyes Jesus Christ was openly portrayed among you as crucified?” (3:1). Bewitched is βασκαίνω (baskaínō, G940) — to put a man under a spell by false representation, a word that carried in the ancient world the whole dread of the evil eye. Paul reaches for it because nothing rational is left to reach for: these people had seen Christ placarded before their eyes as crucified, and they had gone looking for a knife anyway. Only then does he build his case, and he builds it out of the law's own sentences: Abraham, the curse, the tutor, the heir, Hagar and Sarah. Chapters 5 and 6 are the walk — liberty, the Spirit, the flesh, the fruit, the harvest, and a signature scrawled in oversized handwriting: “See with what large letters I write to you with my own hand” (6:11). He took the pen off the secretary at the end because some things you want written in your own fist. And bolted across the seam between the first movement and the second stands the sentence that is the whole letter in miniature: “I have been crucified with Christ, and it is no longer I that live, but Christ lives in me. That life which I now live in the flesh, I live by faith in the Son of God, who loved me, and gave himself up for me” (2:20).

But do not read Galatians as a book with only one enemy, because Paul swings in both directions and he swings hard. Chapter 5 opens with a shout against legalism — “Stand firm therefore in the liberty by which Christ has made us free, and don't be entangled again with a yoke of bondage” (5:1) — and twelve verses later turns and shouts just as loudly at the opposite ditch: “For you, brothers, were called for freedom. Only don't use your freedom for gain to the flesh, but through love be servants to one another” (5:13). The same man. The same chapter. Grace is not a rulebook and it is not a permission slip, and the enemy does not care which side of the road you crash on. And between those two warnings sits the most shocking line Paul ever wrote: “I wish that those who disturb you would cut themselves off” (5:12). Say it plainly, because your Bible does. These men were so enthusiastic about the knife that Paul says he wishes it would slip and take everything — let them go the whole way and mutilate themselves, and be excluded from the assembly of the Lord by their own zeal. It is savage. It is inspired Scripture. And it is not a man losing his temper; it is a shepherd who has watched what a wolf does to sheep, and who would rather be thought unhinged than watch it happen again. Feel that heat as you read. It is the sound of love with nothing to lose. Then let it ask you the only question that matters in this book: what are you still trying to earn from God that He has already handed you for free — and what are you doing with the freedom He gave you instead?

bridge.intro: The Holy Spirit set Galatians immediately after 2 Corinthians because the same war had to be fought one level deeper — first over the messenger, then over the message.

points.title: From “Who Is the True Apostle?” to “What Is the True Gospel?”
points.body: 2 Corinthians was a fight about credentials. Impressive men had walked into Corinth with polish, letters of recommendation and stage presence, and had said of Paul, “For, ‘His letters’, they say, ‘are weighty and strong, but his bodily presence is weak, and his speech is despised.’” (2 Corinthians 10:10). Paul answered by boasting in the one résumé no one else wanted — five floggings, three beatings with rods, a stoning, three shipwrecks (2 Corinthians 11:24–25) — and above all a thorn God would not remove: “My grace is sufficient for you, for my power is made perfect in weakness” (2 Corinthians 12:9). He named the rivals for what they were: “For such men are false apostles, deceitful workers, masquerading as Christ's apostles” (2 Corinthians 11:13), where false apostles is ψευδαπόστολος (pseudapóstolos, G5570). That question — who is the real apostle? — is settled by the time you close 2 Corinthians. Galatians picks the sword straight back up, but the target has moved. Here the counterfeit is not a rival preacher; it is a rival gospel. Paul still defends his commission across chapters 1 and 2, but only as scaffolding — he is not protecting his reputation, he is protecting the message his reputation carries. And watch the escalation, because it tells you everything: in Corinth the danger was men who peddled; in Galatia, Paul says that even if the preacher were himself, or an angel out of heaven, the message would still be cursed. You have just watched a man defend his ministry. Now watch him volunteer to be anathematised rather than let the gospel be edited.

points.title: The Same Two Words, Underlined Twice
points.body: This is not a theme change; it is the same wound reopened, and Paul even uses the same phrase. In Corinth he warned: “For if he who comes preaches another Jesus, whom we did not preach, or if you receive a different spirit, which you did not receive, or a different ‘good news’, which you did not accept, you put up with that well enough” (2 Corinthians 11:4). To Galatia: “deserting him who called you in the grace of Christ to a different ‘good news’” (1:6). The identical word, ἕτερος (héteros, G2087) — not one more of the same kind but another kind entirely. Notice what changed between the two letters. In Corinth Paul's complaint was that they tolerated it: you put up with that well enough. In Galatia tolerance is finished and the verdict is ἀνάθεμα, twice, in four verses. Same virus, later stage, harder medicine. So if you have ever wondered whether Paul's tone in Galatians is out of proportion, lay 2 Corinthians 11:4 beside Galatians 1:6 and you are looking at a man who warned quietly once, and is now shouting because the thing he warned about has walked through the door.

points.title: From the God of All Comfort to the Fire Alarm
points.body: 2 Corinthians is the most emotionally exposed letter in the New Testament, and it opens by blessing God for consolation: “Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Father of mercies and God of all comfort; who comforts us in all our affliction, that we may be able to comfort those who are in any affliction, through the comfort with which we ourselves are comforted by God” (2 Corinthians 1:3–4). Comfort is the word that runs like a river through that entire letter. Then turn one page. Galatians has no blessing, no thanksgiving, no consolation — nothing but a greeting and an accusation. And you must not read that as a colder heart, because chapter 4 shows you a man doubled over: “My little children, of whom I am again in travail until Christ is formed in you—” (4:19). Travail is ὠδίνω (ōdínō, G5605), the word for a woman's labour contractions; formed is μορφόω (morphóō, G3445), the word for shaping something until it takes its true form. He is not less tender here. He is in labour. Comfort is what you give a wounded man; an alarm is what you give a sleeping one. 2 Corinthians is the bandage. Galatians is the shout.

points.title: From Weakness as Proof to the Cross as the Only Boast
points.body: 2 Corinthians demolished boasting in ministry: “Therefore I take pleasure in weaknesses, in injuries, in necessities, in persecutions, in distresses, for Christ's sake. For when I am weak, then am I strong” (2 Corinthians 12:10). Galatians demolishes boasting in salvation: “But far be it from me to boast, except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ, through which the world has been crucified to me, and I to the world” (6:14). And notice where both letters finally land — on Paul's own body. In 2 Corinthians that body carries a thorn he begged God three times to remove and was told to keep. In Galatians the same body carries brand-marks: “I bear the marks of the Lord Jesus branded on my body” (6:17). The flesh that proved he was no super-apostle now proves whose slave he is. Two letters, one verdict, and it lands on you: nothing you can display gets you standing before God — not your gifting, and not your obedience. In 2 Corinthians God took the platform away from you. In Galatians He takes the ladder away too. What is left in your hands after both letters is a cross you did not carry and a life you did not buy.

coreTheme.title: If Righteousness Is Through the Law, Then Christ Died for Nothing
paragraphs: The whole letter is a wheel, and this is the axle. Paul has just finished describing the ugliest scene of his ministry — Peter withdrawing from the Gentile table in Antioch out of fear, the other Jewish believers following him, Barnabas swept along with them — and he says he confronted the chief apostle in front of everybody: “I resisted him to his face, because he stood condemned” (2:11). The speech that follows ends with the sentence the rest of this book will spend four chapters proving: “I don't reject the grace of God. For if righteousness is through the law, then Christ died for nothing!” (2:21). Reject is ἀθετέω (athetéō, G114) — to set aside, to nullify, the word you would use for voiding a contract. And for nothing is δωρεάν (dōreán, G1432), the very word that elsewhere means freely, as a gift — here it lands as needlessly, to no purpose, for nothing at all. Paul's logic is terrifyingly simple and it has no back door. If a person can be made right with God by keeping rules, then the crucifixion was the most extravagant waste in the history of the universe — an unnecessary execution God arranged for His own Son. There is no third option available. Either Calvary was required, or it was pointless. Every time you try to add something to it, you have quietly chosen the second answer.

Then watch how Paul proves it, because he does not argue from feeling — he makes the law testify against itself. Abraham was counted righteous centuries before Sinai and before the knife: “Even as Abraham ‘believed God, and it was counted to him for righteousness.’” (3:6). Then the law speaks its own verdict: “For as many as are of the works of the law are under a curse. For it is written, ‘Cursed is everyone who doesn't continue in all things that are written in the book of the law, to do them.’” (3:10) — all things, continually, not most things, mostly. Then the prophets: “Now that no man is justified by the law before God is evident, for, ‘The righteous will live by faith.’” (3:11). David, you have met that sentence before. It was handed to a prophet standing on a watchtower in the dark, sick of watching violence go unanswered, and told to write it plainly (Habakkuk 2:4). Paul reaches back six centuries, picks it up, and uses it as a crowbar. And then he shows you the exchange: “Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law, having become a curse for us. For it is written, ‘Cursed is everyone who hangs on a tree,’” (3:13). Redeemed is ἐξαγοράζω (exagorázō, G1805) — to buy a slave out of the market and walk him out the door. The law never lowered its demand by one letter. The demand was met in full, on a body, on a Roman stake.

The sentence did not stop moving. Within a year or two of this letter, the Jerusalem Council would rule Paul's way and free the Gentiles (Acts 15). Years later he would say the same thing to Rome in cooler ink: “Because by the works of the law, no flesh will be justified in his sight... But now apart from the law, a righteousness of God has been revealed” (Romans 3:20–21), and, “For Christ is the fulfillment of the law for righteousness to everyone who believes” (Romans 10:4). Then history caught fire. Martin Luther lectured on Galatians in 1519 and again in 1531, and in his Table Talk he said that Galatians was his own epistle, that he had betrothed himself to it — it is my Katharina, he said, naming his wife. The Reformation was, in very large part, this letter read out loud in public. So trace the chain and do not forget it: a prophet on a watchtower, a furious apostle dictating in a hurry to four small towns in Asia Minor, a monk in a German lecture hall, and a believer in Ghana reading it tonight on a screen. One sentence. Still burning. Nobody has ever improved on it.

So bring it home, and be brutal about it, because this is where the doctrine either becomes yours or stays on the page. You almost certainly do not believe you are saved by circumcision. But watch your own mechanisms. Have you ever fasted mainly to shorten the odds on an answer? Do you find yourself rehearsing what you have done for God before you ask Him for anything, the way a man recites his years of service before he asks for a raise? When you fail badly, is your first instinct to run to the blood — or to go and do something good enough to cancel it out? And when somebody else falls publicly, is there a quiet flicker of standing in you, as though grace were a league table and you were doing rather well in it? Every one of those is a sentence spoken quietly over Calvary: not quite enough. That is what makes Galatians so uncomfortable. It does not catch you denying the cross. It catches you decorating it. And you cannot add to a finished work — you can only insult it.

truths.intro: As we journey through these 6 chapters, the Holy Spirit wants to anchor these truths in your spirit:

items.title: The Gospel Cannot Survive an “And”
items.body: The men troubling Galatia were not preaching Jesus-minus. They were preaching Jesus-plus, and that is far more dangerous, because it sounds like extra devotion. Paul does the arithmetic for you and it is merciless: “Behold, I, Paul, tell you that if you receive circumcision, Christ will profit you nothing” (5:2); “Yes, I testify again to every man who receives circumcision, that he is a debtor to do the whole law” (5:3); “You are alienated from Christ, you who desire to be justified by the law. You have fallen away from grace” (5:4). Take one item onto your account and you have opened an account — and the account demands everything. Then he gives the picture: “A little yeast grows through the whole lump” (5:9). Yeast is ζύμη (zýmē, G2219), and nobody has ever added a little yeast intending to change the whole loaf; that is simply what yeast does, quietly, overnight, everywhere. Grace will not share the throne. It either saves you entirely or it does not save you at all. So find your “and.” It will not be circumcision. It will be the attendance record, the giving streak, the years since the old life, the fluency of your prayers, the ministry title, the fact that you are the responsible one in your family. Here is the test: if God asked you tonight why He should receive you, what would come out of your mouth before the blood of Jesus? Whatever that is — that is your yeast. Kill it now, before chapter 3, because Paul is about to ask the Galatians the question he is really asking you: “Having begun in the Spirit, are you now completed in the flesh?” (3:3). Completed is ἐπιτελέω (epiteléō, G2005), to bring to full finish. You were not saved by grace and then handed a performance system to keep the verdict alive.

items.title: The Law Was Never the Ladder — It Was the Tutor Who Walked You to Christ
items.body: Paul is not anti-law, and he stops the accusation before you can make it: “Is the law then against the promises of God? Certainly not! For if there had been a law given which could make alive, most certainly righteousness would have been of the law” (3:21). The law is not the villain of this letter. It is a good thing doing a specific job — “It was added because of transgressions, until the offspring should come to whom the promise has been made” (3:19) — and then he names the job with one unforgettable word: “So that the law has become our tutor to bring us to Christ, that we might be justified by faith. But now that faith has come, we are no longer under a tutor” (3:24–25). Tutor is παιδαγωγός (paidagōgós, G3807), and it does not mean schoolteacher. In a wealthy Greco-Roman household the paidagōgos was a trusted slave assigned to a boy: he walked the child to school every morning, carried his tablets, corrected his manners, disciplined him when he needed it, and kept him out of trouble — and the day the boy came of age, that man's authority over him simply ended. The law walked humanity to the schoolroom door and handed us over. It was never the ladder to God. It was the escort to the Saviour. And look at what waits on the other side of the door: “But when the fullness of the time came, God sent out his Son, born to a woman, born under the law, that he might redeem those who were under the law, that we might receive the adoption of children. And because you are children, God sent out the Spirit of his Son into your hearts, crying, ‘Abba, Father!’ So you are no longer a bondservant, but a son; and if a son, then an heir of God through Christ” (4:4–7). Adoption is υἱοθεσία (huiothesía, G5206), a Roman legal act that lifted a person out of one family and placed him in another with full standing and full inheritance rights. And the proof God gives you is not a certificate — it is a cry. Ἀββᾶ (Abbâ, G5) is Aramaic, the word a child says at home, left untranslated in a Greek letter because the Spirit had taught Gentile mouths the family word. That is the tragedy of Galatia in one line: they had the Father's name in their mouths and were reaching back for the tutor's rod. “But now that you have come to know God, or rather to be known by God, why do you turn back again to the weak and miserable elemental principles, to which you desire to be in bondage all over again?” (4:9). Elemental principles is στοιχεῖον (stoicheîon, G4747) — the ABCs, the beginner's basics — and notice the shocking thing Paul does with it: he uses the same word for the pagan idolatry they came out of and for the law-keeping they are running toward. Two different cages. Identical bars.

items.title: Freedom Is Not a Longer Leash — It Is a New Master and a New Walk
items.body: “Stand firm therefore in the liberty by which Christ has made us free, and don't be entangled again with a yoke of bondage” (5:1). Liberty is ἐλευθερία (eleuthería, G1657), the status of a free citizen rather than a slave; yoke is ζυγός (zygós, G2218), the beam laid across an animal's neck to make it pull what its owner chooses. Christ did not renegotiate your slavery. He ended it. But read the next paragraph before you celebrate, because Paul turns and takes aim at the opposite ditch: “For you, brothers, were called for freedom. Only don't use your freedom for gain to the flesh, but through love be servants to one another” (5:13). Gain is ἀφορμή (aphormḗ, G874) — a base of operations, a bridgehead, the staging ground from which an army launches its attack. Your flesh, σάρξ (sárx, G4561), is not neutral about your liberty; it is looking for a place to land troops. And Paul's answer to that is not a new list of rules; it is a new gait. “But I say, walk by the Spirit, and you won't fulfill the lust of the flesh” (5:16) — walk is περιπατέω (peripatéō, G4043), to conduct your ordinary daily life. Then at the end of the chapter he swaps the verb: “If we live by the Spirit, let's also walk by the Spirit” (5:25), and that one is στοιχέω (stoichéō, G4748), to march in rank, to keep step in formation. Not drifting in the general direction of the Spirit — keeping step with Him, one deliberate foot at a time. And what grows on that road is not a list of achievements but produce: “But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faith, gentleness, and self-control. Against such things there is no law” (5:22–23). Fruit is καρπός (karpós, G2590), and it is singular — one fruit with nine facets, not a buffet where you take the two you are naturally good at and skip self-control. Meanwhile the flesh does not get managed; it gets executed: “Those who belong to Christ have crucified the flesh with its passions and lusts” (5:24) — the echo of 2:20, where crucified with Him is συσταυρόω (systauróō, G4957). Then chapter 6 refuses to let any of this float free of your Monday: “Bear one another's burdens, and so fulfill the law of Christ” (6:2), and, “Don't be deceived. God is not mocked, for whatever a man sows, that he will also reap. For he who sows to his own flesh will from the flesh reap corruption. But he who sows to the Spirit will from the Spirit reap eternal life” (6:7–8). Grace did not repeal the harvest. It changed which field you are sowing in. And the final word on all of it: “For in Christ Jesus neither is circumcision anything, nor uncircumcision, but a new creation” (6:15) — κτίσις (ktísis, G2937), a brand-new act of making. God is not renovating you into a better law-keeper. He has started something from scratch.

preparation.intro: Before we step into Chapter 1, prepare your spirit with these reflections:

items.title: The Ledger You Are Still Keeping
items.body: Do not answer this with what you believe on paper. Answer it with what your prayer life actually does. Is your confidence before God different on a week you have done well than on a week you have failed? Do you pray longer before a big request, half-hoping the length buys you a hearing? Do you avoid Him for three days after a fall, as though the waiting were part of the payment? Do you feel more like a son on Sunday evening than at 2am on Tuesday? Every one of those is a receipt from a ledger you are still keeping, and Galatians has come to burn the book. So take a sheet of paper tonight and write down the top three things you have quietly been paying God with. Be specific and be embarrassed — that is the point. Then write one sentence across the whole list, out loud, in your own voice: “I have been crucified with Christ, and it is no longer I that live, but Christ lives in me” (2:20). Then ask the Holy Spirit the harder question underneath the first one, because chapter 1 will ask it before you get out of the room: whose approval are you actually farming — God's, or somebody's? “For am I now seeking the favor of men, or of God? Or am I striving to please men? For if I were still pleasing men, I wouldn't be a servant of Christ” (1:10). Most legalism is not really about God at all. It is about being seen as the kind of person who has it together.

items.title: The Other Ditch
items.body: Paul swings in both directions inside a single chapter, and the reflection above dealt with the first ditch. This one is for the second — the ditch nobody warns you about, because it wears the vocabulary of grace while it does its work: “don't use your freedom for gain to the flesh, but through love be servants to one another” (5:13). Name your version of it before you begin. Where have you used the word grace as a permission slip? Which appetite have you fed with a verse in your mouth? Which conversation have you refused to have, which apology have you not made, which habit have you renamed a weakness so you would not have to call it sin? Then read the line most people skip, because it sits two verses later on purpose: “But if you bite and devour one another, be careful that you don't consume one another” (5:15). The picture is animals tearing at each other in a pit, and Paul puts it directly after the great freedom text, because the first thing unshepherded freedom does is turn on people. So ask the Spirit for one name — the relative you talk about, the leader you criticise, the person you win arguments against. Then decide, before you read chapter 1, on one concrete act of servanthood you will do for that exact person this week. Paul's phrase is “through love be servants to one another,” and the verb is δουλεύω (douleúō, G1398), to serve as a slave serves. A freed man volunteering for the collar. That, and not a longer leash, is what Christian liberty looks like when it stands up and walks.

prayerOfActivation: Father, I open this letter and I already feel the heat coming off the page. Before I read a word of chapter 1, search me — because I am the kind of man who tries to pay for what You have already given. You know the ledger I have been keeping. You have watched me pray more boldly on my good weeks and hide from You on my bad ones, as though Your welcome went up and down with my performance. Lord, I lay the book down. I stop paying. I receive what I cannot earn. Thank You for the Son who gave Himself for my sins, to deliver me out of this present evil age, according to Your will. Thank You that the message did not come from a committee and does not belong to any man — so no man can change it, and no man can take it from me. Holy Spirit, make me a person who will not tolerate a different gospel, not in a pulpit, not in a book, and not in my own head at midnight. Show me my “and” — every hidden thing I would name to You before the blood of Jesus — and let it die in Your presence tonight. Teach me the truth of the tutor: that the law was never my ladder, that it walked me to Christ and its authority over me ended at His feet, and that I am no longer a bondservant but a son, and if a son, then an heir. Put the family word in my mouth again. Abba, Father. Lord Jesus, I have been crucified with You. It is no longer I that live, but You who live in me; and the life I now live in this body, I live by faith in the Son of God, who loved me and gave Himself up for me. So I refuse the yoke of bondage on one side and the leash of the flesh on the other. Do not let me use Your grace as a staging ground for anything I would be ashamed to name. Where I have been biting and devouring the people closest to me, forgive me, and make me a servant to them in love. Spirit of God, teach me to walk in step with You — not drifting in Your general direction, but marching in rank, one deliberate day at a time — until the fruit is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faith, gentleness and self-control, and not the two of those I happen to be good at. Where I have sown to the flesh, stop the harvest; where I have grown weary in doing good, hold me up until due season. I will not give up. And when this letter is finished in me, let there be nothing left to boast about except the cross of my Lord Jesus Christ, through which the world has been crucified to me, and I to the world. I am not being renovated. I am a new creation. Brand me as Yours, Lord — let my scars, my history and my whole life read as the marks of Jesus on my body. In the mighty name of Jesus, Amen!
